title: Connect hospitality to the event programme
focus: Food should support the transitions in a company event: arrival, networking, formal presentations and the closing period. Decide which moments need passed bites, a meal or simply refreshments. A launch reception and staff celebration may use similar ingredients but require different service rhythms. Share the venue plan and the programme together so catering stations do not interrupt key activities. Confirm the team, equipment and service hours in one proposal that the organiser and venue can both work from.

sections.title: Match the food service to the event programme
paragraphs: A product launch needs a different service rhythm from a staff celebration. During a reveal or presentation, trays and clearing should pause. During networking, passed canapés can keep guests moving, while a staffed buffet gives a longer gathering a clear meal period. Share the programme before choosing the menu.

The catering brief should describe the audience as well as the headcount. Include arrival patterns, dietary requirements and whether the food replaces dinner or supports a short reception. If guests will move between rooms, identify where food may be served and where the team can prepare, store and replenish it.

Agree the arrival window, catering equipment, service hours and collection arrangements with the venue. Bar services and additional event requirements should appear as separate items where requested. For the food itself, compare a canapé menu with live cooking stations and choose the format that supports the occasion.

sections.title: Match the bites to the length of the reception
paragraphs: Tell us whether the reception food is a welcome before dinner or the main food for the event. The same list of bites will not suit both jobs. Share the reception length, guest count and any later meal before deciding the balance of small bites and more substantial dishes.

Think about how people will move between registration, networking and presentations. Passed food needs a route through the room, while a buffet needs a serving area that will not obstruct the programme. Confirm where drinks, used glasses and dietary alternatives will be handled.

If the event includes speeches or awards, agree when service should pause and when the final food will be offered. Put the agreed food quantities, staff roles and service hours in the proposal so the event team can assess the complete scope.

links.label: Compare a buffet for the event

sections.title: Build the service schedule around your guests
paragraphs: Work backwards from the time guests should begin eating. The team may need access earlier for unloading, setup and preparation, particularly when equipment or several service areas are involved. Share the programme before the menu is finalised so the catering plan can support it.

Identify moments when service should pause, such as a speech, presentation or ceremony. For an office event, confirm the length of each break and whether everyone will arrive at once. For a private celebration, allow for the welcome period and any cake or toast that needs its own place in the sequence.

Agree a contact for changes on the day. Small timing adjustments may be manageable, while a substantial extension can affect staffing and the booked hours. Clear communication helps the team respond sensibly and keeps the food connected to the occasion rather than running on a separate timetable.
